related_questions.question: How long does food poisoning last?

text_blocks.snippet: Food poisoning symptoms typically last from a few hours to several days, with most cases resolving within 12 to 48 hours. However, some infections, like those caused by parasites, can extend symptoms for a week or more. The duration can also vary based on the specific germ causing the illness and individual factors.
snippet_highlighted_words: a few hours to several days, with most cases resolving within 12 to 48 hours

list.title: Type of germ:
list.snippet: Bacterial infections may last 1-7 days, while viral infections often resolve within 1-3 days, and parasitic infections can last longer.

list.title: Severity of the illness:
list.snippet: Mild cases may resolve quickly, while severe cases may require medical intervention and longer recovery periods.

list.title: Individual factors:
list.snippet: Age, overall health, and immune system strength can affect how long symptoms last.

related_questions.question: How does the ER treat food poisoning?

text_blocks.snippet: In the ER, food poisoning treatment focuses on managing symptoms and preventing complications, primarily through rehydration and addressing severe cases with antibiotics or other targeted medications. Most cases can be managed at home, but severe symptoms like persistent vomiting, bloody stools, or signs of dehydration warrant ER care.
snippet_highlighted_words: rehydration and addressing severe cases with antibiotics or other targeted medications

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at the ER approach:

list.title: Symptom evaluation:
list.snippet: Doctors will ask about your symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea, fever, etc.) and recent food intake to determine the potential cause.

list.title: Physical exam:
list.snippet: Vital signs (temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, etc.) will be checked, according to Veterans Health Library.

list.title: Lab tests:
list.snippet: Blood, urine, and stool samples may be taken to identify the specific bacteria, virus, or parasite causing the illness and to assess for dehydration or other complications.

list.title: Rehydration:
list.snippet: The primary focus is replenishing lost fluids and electrolytes due to vomiting and diarrhea. This is often done through IV fluids, especially in severe cases.
Anti-nausea medications: To alleviate nausea and vomiting, providing relief and aiding in fluid retention, according to Advance ER.
Antibiotics: Prescribed only if the infection is confirmed to be bacterial (e.g., E. coli, Listeria, Salmonella) and is severe or poses a high risk of complications.
Antiparasitics: Used for parasitic infections.

list.title: Observation:
list.snippet: In severe cases, patients may be monitored closely in the ER or even admitted to the hospital until their symptoms improve.

list.title: Pain management:
list.snippet: Over-the-counter or prescription pain relievers may be used to manage abdominal cramps and other discomfort.
Severe dehydration: Signs include infrequent urination, dry mouth and throat, and dizziness upon standing.
Persistent vomiting or diarrhea: Especially if you can't keep down fluids.
High fever: Temperature over 102°F.
Bloody vomit or stools: According to the CDC.
Signs of infection: Such as a severe headache, stiff neck, or confusion.
Underlying health conditions: Individuals with weakened immune systems, pregnant women, or those with other health issues are at higher risk of complications and should seek medical attention sooner.

text_blocks.snippet: 4. What to Expect After ER Visit:

list.snippet: Discharge instructions: You'll receive guidance on how to manage your symptoms at home, including recommendations for diet and fluid intake.
Medications: If prescribed, you'll receive instructions on how to take them.
Follow-up care: If needed, you'll be advised to follow up with your primary care physician for further monitoring.

related_questions.question: How to tell if it's food poisoning or stomach bug?

text_blocks.snippet: It can be tricky to tell the difference between food poisoning and a stomach bug (viral gastroenteritis), as they share similar symptoms like nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and stomach cramps. However, the key distinction lies in the speed of symptom onset and duration. Food poisoning symptoms typically appear quickly, within hours of consuming contaminated food, while stomach bug symptoms develop more gradually over a day or two. Food poisoning also tends to be shorter in duration, often resolving within a day or two, whereas a stomach bug can last for several days.
snippet_highlighted_words: Food poisoning symptoms typically appear quickly, within hours of consuming contaminated food, while stomach bug symptoms develop more gradually over a day or two

text_blocks.snippet: Most food poisoning cases are mild and can be managed at home with rest, hydration, and a bland diet. However, if symptoms are severe, persistent, or accompanied by certain warning signs, seeking medical attention is crucial.
snippet_highlighted_words: rest, hydration, and a bland diet

text_blocks.snippet: Home Care for Mild Food Poisoning:

list.title: Rest:
list.snippet: Allow your body to recover by getting plenty of sleep.

list.title: Hydration:
list.snippet: Drink plenty of fluids to replace those lost through vomiting and diarrhea. Oral rehydration solutions like Pedialyte are particularly helpful.

list.title: Bland Diet:
list.snippet: Start with easily digestible foods like toast, crackers, rice, and bananas when you feel ready to eat.

list.title: Avoid:
list.snippet: Dairy, caffeine, alcohol, spicy or fatty foods, and sugary drinks, as these can worsen symptoms.
Prolonged vomiting or diarrhea: If vomiting lasts more than two days or diarrhea lasts for more than a few days, consult a doctor.
Bloody or black stools: These can indicate a more serious issue.
High fever: A fever of 101°F (38.3°C) or higher warrants medical attention.
Severe dehydration: Symptoms like dizziness, lightheadedness, or confusion can indicate severe dehydration.
Severe abdominal pain: Seek immediate medical care for intense stomach pain.
Confusion or altered mental state: Any changes in mental clarity or alertness should be evaluated by a doctor.
Rehydration: In severe cases, intravenous fluids and electrolytes may be needed to combat dehydration.
Antibiotics: If bacterial infection is confirmed, antibiotics may be prescribed.
Antiparasitic medication: If a parasitic infection is the cause, antiparasitic drugs may be necessary.
Probiotics: Your doctor may recommend probiotics to help restore healthy gut bacteria.

list.title: Infants and young children:
list.snippet: Are more vulnerable to dehydration and may require specific care, including electrolyte solutions and close monitoring.

list.title: Older adults and those with weakened immune systems:
list.snippet: Are also at higher risk for complications from food poisoning and should seek medical attention promptly.
